texts.title: Before the change
texts.text: Rosa remembers her office life the way you remember an old coat: familiar, slightly tight. She used to commute ninety minutes each way. She used to eat lunch at her desk and answer emails at midnight. 'I used to think that was normal,' she says. 'Everyone around me did the same.' Two years ago she moved to a small town and opened a bookshop. At first, the silence was unbearable — she didn't use to have quiet, and it felt like something was wrong. Now she closes at six and reads in the evenings. 'People ask if I miss the city. Although I loved parts of it, I don't miss the person I was becoming there.'

texts.title: The Monday pool
texts.text: Every Monday, the design team runs a small prediction pool. 'Ten euros says the client changes the brief by Wednesday,' says Jonas. Petra shakes her head. 'The brief will survive — but the printer will break. It always does.' Newcomer Ana smiles nervously. 'I'll just predict something safe: we'll all complain about the coffee.' Everyone writes their bets on the whiteboard, and the week starts. By Wednesday, the client has indeed changed the brief, twice. Jonas collects his ten euros without a word. The printer, loyal to tradition, jams on Thursday morning — Petra's turn to smile. And on Friday, Ana looks at her line on the board, at the empty coffee machine, and says what everyone is thinking: 'Will anyone else complain, or is it just me?'

texts.title: The rumour mill
texts.text: Carmen came back from one day off and the office had invented three futures. 'Marco said the company was moving to Lisbon,' whispered Diego. 'Lena told me they were hiring twenty people,' said Carmen. 'And Priya swears she heard we were all getting new laptops.' Carmen put down her bag and applied the office rule: trace every rumour to its source. The Lisbon story started with a photo Marco took of a moving van — which was moving his neighbour's piano. The twenty hires were real, but Lena had read 'over the next five years' and skipped that part. And the laptops were true: an email had gone out at seven that morning. One truth, one exaggeration, one piano.

texts.title: Grandpa's garden
texts.text: When Pablo was a child, he spent every summer at his grandpa's house. The garden was enormous, full of tomato plants and lemon trees. Every morning they watered the plants together and every afternoon they played cards under the big tree. His grandpa didn't talk much, but he laughed easily. Pablo didn't like vegetables then. Now he grows his own tomatoes and understands why his grandpa smiled at them.

texts.text: Last week Daniel lost his favourite jacket. He left it on the number twelve bus on Friday evening. He called the lost property office on Monday, but nobody had seen it. texts.title: The night train
texts.text: Ella took the night train to the coast because the morning tickets were too expensive. She shared a small compartment with a woman who worked as a nurse and a student who talked for hours about football. Ella couldn't sleep, but she didn't mind. The train arrived at five in the morning, before the sun came up. She walked out of the station, smelled the sea and knew the trip was worth it.

texts.title: The four-day week
texts.text: At the town-hall debate, both speakers agreed on the problem — burnout — and disagreed on nearly everything else. The union representative argued that a four-day week was the obvious fix: trials in Iceland, she said, had been judged a success by almost every measure, and productivity had been maintained with happier staff. The chamber-of-commerce speaker pushed back. Those trials, he replied, were small and self-selected; forcing the change on small businesses could raise costs and reduce service hours. An audience member proposed the middle path nobody had mentioned: keep five contract days but cut meetings by half. Both speakers, perhaps unexpectedly, said they could live with that — which is usually the sign of a good compromise.

texts.title: The salary standoff
texts.text: 'Let's start with the number you want, and I'll tell you honestly if it's possible,' said the manager. Nadia appreciated the directness. 'Forty-eight thousand — that's the market rate for this role, and I can show you three listings that prove it.' The manager didn't flinch. 'I believe you. If I approved that today, I'd have to rewrite three other salaries, and I don't have the budget for that this quarter.' 'What if we phased it?' Nadia offered. 'Forty-four now, a review in March with clear targets, and forty-eight if I hit them.' The manager was quiet for a moment. 'If you put those targets in writing and hit them, I'll defend that raise upstairs. Shall we say we have a deal?' Nadia smiled. 'We have a deal — in writing.'

texts.title: The morning news: bridge reopened
texts.text: Good morning. The Millbrook bridge, which was closed in March after cracks were discovered in two support beams, was reopened to traffic shortly after six this morning — three weeks ahead of schedule. Repair work, which was carried out by a local firm, was funded jointly by the council and the regional government, though the exact split has not been disclosed. Drivers are being asked to observe the fifty-kilometre limit for the first fortnight while the surface settles. Bus route nine, which was diverted via the ring road, returns to its original route today. And in a surprise twist, the ferry that was launched as a temporary replacement — will keep running until September, after commuters, apparently, fell in love with it.

texts.title: Podcast: the habits episode
texts.text: HOST: Welcome back. Today, habits — the ones that stick and the ones that don't. With me, Dr Amaia Ruiz, who has spent a decade researching behaviour. Amaia, quick version: why do most New Year's resolutions fail? DR RUIZ: Because they're ambitions, not systems. People say 'I'll get fit' — that's a wish. A system is 'I run on Tuesdays with Sam.' HOST: So the friend is part of the system? DR RUIZ: The friend is the system. Accountability beats motivation roughly nine times out of ten in our data. HOST: Nine out of ten! And the two-minute rule everyone quotes? DR RUIZ: Useful, slightly overrated. Starting small matters less than starting at the same time. The clock does the remembering for you. HOST: One habit you'd recommend to everyone? DR RUIZ: A ten-minute walk after lunch. Boring, free, and — according to everything we know — the closest thing to a miracle we've measured.

texts.title: The keynote
texts.text: Good afternoon. I'd like to begin with a confession: everything I believed about attention five years ago has aged badly. The research I'll present today — conducted across four countries, with the caveats that such breadth demands — suggests something uncomfortable: our capacity for sustained focus hasn't declined so much as our tolerance for discomfort has collapsed. Now, I appreciate that's a strong claim. The evidence runs like this. In conditions where devices were removed — not silenced, removed — reading comprehension recovered to pre-smartphone baselines within nine days. What participants reported, however, was not relief but a kind of withdrawal, which raises the question I'd like to leave you with: if a tool has rewritten our baseline for what feels bearable, is it a tool any more? I'll let you sit with that. Thank you.
